questions.question: Which changes can UI policy actions make to a field on a form? (Choose three.)

options.text: Make it mandatory
Make it visible or hidden
Make it read-only
Encrypt its value in the database
Change its column data type

explanation.correct: UI policies change form behavior dynamically, for example making fields read-only or mandatory, or hiding them. UI Policy Actions have Mandatory, Visible, and Read only choice lists (Leave alone, True, False). See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/t_CreateAUIPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policies run in the browser and don't encrypt data.
Data types are defined in the dictionary.

source.excerpt: make the number field on a form read-only, make the short description field mandatory, and hide other fields

questions.question: An administrator can use either a client script or a UI policy to make a field mandatory. According to ServiceNow, why should they prefer the UI policy when possible?

options.text: UI policies give faster load times
UI policies also secure the data on the server
UI policies work in every API integration
UI policies can't be overridden by ACLs

explanation.correct: Client scripts can do everything UI policies do, but ServiceNow recommends UI policies when possible for faster load times. Basic UI policies need no scripting. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/t_CreateAUIPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policies run on the client and aren't a data security control.
UI policies apply to forms in the UI, not to integrations; data policies cover other data sources.
ACLs and UI policies do different jobs.

source.excerpt: You can also use client scripts to perform all of these actions, but for faster load times use UI policies when possible.

questions.question: A UI policy has Reverse if false selected. What happens when its conditions change from true to false?

options.text: The UI policy actions are undone
Nothing; the actions remain
The form is submitted
The record is deleted

explanation.correct: With Reverse if false selected, the UI policy actions run when the conditions are true and are undone when they evaluate to false. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/t_CreateAUIPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: That describes Reverse if false being cleared.
UI policies don't submit forms.
UI policies don't delete records.

source.excerpt: Option for specifying that the UI policy action is undone when the conditions of its UI policy evaluate to false.

questions.question: A UI policy should make Additional comments mandatory only when a user changes State to Awaiting user info, not every time a record already in that state is opened. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Clear the On load check box
Select Global
Select Inherit
Set the Order to 1

explanation.correct: On load controls whether the UI policy runs every time a form loads when its conditions are met. In the documented example, clearing On load means the policy applies only when the state is changed to Awaiting user info. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/t_CreateAUIPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Global controls whether the policy applies to all form views.
Inherit controls whether extended tables inherit the policy.
Order sets processing sequence when policies conflict.

source.excerpt: clears the On load check box. This condition means that the UI policy applies only when the state is changed to Awaiting user info.

questions.question: Two UI policies on the same table conflict. One has Order 100 and the other has Order 200. Which one's action takes effect?

options.text: The policy with Order 200, because the higher number executes last
The policy with Order 100
Neither; conflicting policies are both skipped
The one created first

explanation.correct: UI policies run from lowest to highest Order. If two policies conflict, the one with the higher number executes. For inherited policies, the child table's policies run first, then the base table's. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/t_CreateAUIPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The lower number runs first and is overridden.
Both policies run.
Creation date doesn't determine precedence.

source.excerpt: If two policies conflict, the UI policy with the higher number executes.

questions.question: When are UI policy conditions rechecked on an open form?

options.text: Only when a user manually changes a field on the form
Every time a UI action runs
Whenever the list editor changes a value
Every 60 seconds

explanation.correct: UI policy conditions are only rechecked when a user manually changes a field on a form. Changes made by a UI action, context menu action, or the list editor are not evaluated. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/t_CreateAUIPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Changes made by UI actions are not evaluated.
List editor changes are not evaluated.
UI policies don't re-evaluate on a timer.

source.excerpt: Conditions are only rechecked if a user manually changes a field on a form.

questions.question: Problems are updated by an external system through web services, and Close notes must be filled in before a problem is closed. The existing UI policy doesn't enforce this. What should the administrator use?

options.text: A data policy
Another UI policy
A client script
A form template

explanation.correct: UI policies only apply to data entered on a form in the standard browser. Data policies apply to all data entered into the system, including data from import sets, web services, and the mobile UI. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/c_DataPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policies don't apply to web service updates.
Client scripts run in the browser and don't affect web service updates.
Templates prefill forms; they don't enforce rules.

source.excerpt: Data policies can apply rules to all data entered into the system, including data brought in through import sets or web services and data entered through the mobile UI.

questions.question: What is a business rule?

options.text: A server-side script that runs when a record is displayed, inserted, updated, or deleted, or when a table is queried
A client-side script that runs when a form loads
A rule that assigns tasks to groups without scripting
A security rule that controls access to records

explanation.correct: A business rule is a server-side script that runs when a record is displayed, inserted, updated, or deleted, or when a table is queried. ServiceNow now recommends Workflow Studio for new process automation. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Client-side form scripts are client scripts.
Assignment without scripting uses assignment or data lookup rules.
Access is controlled by ACLs.

source.excerpt: A business rule is a server-side script that runs when a record is displayed, inserted, updated, or deleted, or when a table is queried.

questions.question: A business rule must set a field value on the current record before it is saved to the database. Which When value should it use?

options.text: Before
After
Async
Display

explanation.correct: Before business rules run after the user submits the form but before any action is taken on the record in the database. Changes made in before rules are saved automatically, so you don't need current.update(). See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: After rules run after the database action and are best for updating related records.
Async rules run later as scheduled jobs.
Display rules run when the form is loaded, before it's shown to the user.

source.excerpt: After the user submits the form but before any action is taken on the record in the database.

questions.question: When does a Display business rule run?

options.text: Before the form is shown to the user, just after the data is read from the database
After the record is saved
When the scheduler runs a job
When the user logs out

explanation.correct: Display business rules run before the form is presented to the user, just after the data is read from the database. They are often used to populate g_scratchpad for client scripts. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: That describes After rules.
That describes Async rules.
Business rules aren't tied to logout.

source.excerpt: Before the form is presented to the user, just after the data is read from the database.

questions.question: Why does ServiceNow advise against calling current.update() in a business rule script?

options.text: It can make business rules run again on the same table, causing recursion
It deletes the record
It is blocked for all administrators
It only works in client scripts

explanation.correct: Avoid current.update() in business rules. It triggers business rules on the same table for insert and update, which can make a rule call itself over and over. Changes in before rules are saved automatically, and after rules are best for updating related records. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: update() saves the record; it doesn't delete it.
Admins can call it, but it's discouraged.
current.update() is a server-side call.

source.excerpt: Avoid using current.update() in a business rule script.

questions.question: How do business rules differ from client scripts in when they apply? (Choose two.)

options.text: Business rules apply to records whether they are accessed through forms, lists, or web services
Client scripts apply only when the form is edited
Business rules run only in the browser
Client scripts run on the server after the database operation

explanation.correct: Business rules apply consistently to records whether they're accessed through forms, lists, or web services. That's a major difference from client scripts, which apply only when the form is edited. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Business rules run on the server.
Client scripts run in the browser.

source.excerpt: Business rules apply consistently to records regardless of whether they are accessed through forms, lists, or web services.

questions.question: Which actions can administrators configure in a business rule without writing a script? (Choose three.)

options.text: Set field values
Create information messages
Abort the transaction
Call an external REST API
Create a new table

explanation.correct: Administrators can set field values, create information messages, and abort transactions without writing a script. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Calling external APIs needs scripting or Integration Hub.
Tables are created in System Definition, not by business rules.

source.excerpt: Administrators can set field values, create information messages, and abort transactions without writing a script.

questions.question: Why does ServiceNow recommend script includes instead of global business rules for reusable server functions?

options.text: Script includes load only on request, while global business rules load on every page
Script includes run in the browser
Global business rules can't access GlideRecord
Script includes bypass ACLs

explanation.correct: Script includes load only on request, while global business rules load on every page in the system. That's why script includes are recommended for reusable code. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Script includes run on the server.
Global business rules can use GlideRecord; the concern is performance.
Script includes don't bypass security.

source.excerpt: Script includes load only on request while global business rules load on every page in the system.

questions.question: In the execution order of scripts and engines, what runs immediately before the database operation (insert, update, or delete)?

options.text: Before business rules with an order of 1000 or more
After business rules with an order below 1000
Email notifications
Async business rules

explanation.correct: The order is: before rules with order below 1000, then before engines, then before rules with order of 1000 or more, then the database operation, then after rules with order below 1000, after engines, email notifications, and after rules with order of 1000 or more. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/r_ExecutionOrderScriptsAndEngines.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: After rules run after the database operation.
Notifications run after the database operation and after engines.
Async rules run in the background after the operation.

documentation.section: Execution order of scripts and engines

source.excerpt: Before business rules: Scripts configured to execute before the database operation with an order greater than or equal to 1000.

questions.question: What is an update set?

options.text: A group of configuration changes that can be moved from one instance to another
A backup of all instance data
A set of records imported from a spreadsheet
A list of pending platform upgrades

explanation.correct: An update set is a group of configuration changes that can be moved between instances. Developers create functionality on a non-production instance and promote the changes to another instance for testing or deployment. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/exploring-system-update-sets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Update sets hold configuration changes, not all data.
Imported records go through import sets.
Upgrades aren't delivered as update sets.

source.excerpt: An update set is a group of configuration changes that can be moved from one instance to another.

questions.question: An administrator orders a catalog item on the development instance while building it. Which of these does the update set capture?

options.text: The catalog item definition and its variables, but not the submitted order or catalog tasks
The submitted order and catalog tasks only
Both the definition and all submitted orders
Nothing, because catalog items can't be captured

explanation.correct: Update sets capture configuration details but not task or process data. They record catalog item definitions, variables, and variable choices, but not submitted orders or catalog tasks. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/customizations-tracked-update-sets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Orders and tasks are process data, which isn't captured.
Submitted orders are process data.
Catalog item definitions are captured.

source.excerpt: Update sets capture configuration details but exclude task or process data.

questions.question: What does ServiceNow recommend for the path update sets take between instances?

options.text: Keep one common path, such as dev to test to production, and never migrate the same update set from multiple sources
Move update sets directly from dev to production to save time
Retrieve the same update set from several instances to compare
Edit update sets on production and move them back to dev

explanation.correct: Pick a common path for update sets to move between instances and stick to it. Never migrate the same update set from multiple sources. Move update sets from dev to test, then from test to production. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/exploring-system-update-sets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Changes should be tested before production.
Never migrate the same update set from multiple sources.
Develop on dev and promote forward.

source.excerpt: Never migrate the same update set from multiple sources.

questions.question: A fix for a problem in update set A was made in update set B. In what order should they be committed on production?

options.text: A, then B, in the order they were made
B, then A
Only B
Either order, because the system sorts them

explanation.correct: If an update set needed a fix, commit both update sets on production in the order they were made. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/exploring-system-update-sets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Committing out of order can overwrite newer changes with older ones.
Both sets must be committed.
The documentation says to commit them in the order they were made.

source.excerpt: If the update set required a fix, commit both update sets in the order they were made.

questions.question: What does previewing a retrieved update set do?

options.text: Checks the retrieved update set against the local instance to find problems that should be resolved before committing
Commits the update set in a sandbox
Sends the update set to the source instance
Deletes older update sets

explanation.correct: Previewing checks a retrieved update set against the local instance to find problems, which you should resolve before committing. Problems appear in the Update Set Preview Problems related list. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/t_PreviewARemoteUpdateSet.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Previewing doesn't commit anything.
Previewing happens on the target instance.
Previewing doesn't delete update sets.

source.excerpt: Previewing checks a retrieved update set against the local instance to find issues. Resolve all problems before committing the update set.

questions.question: How does the platform detect an update set collision?

options.text: It compares the Name and Updated values of the customer update records; the same name with different update dates is a collision
It compares the size of the update sets
It checks whether both update sets have the same description
It compares the sys_created_by field

explanation.correct: A collision is an update that has a newer local update. The platform compares the Name and Updated fields of the customer update record from each update set. If the names match but the update dates differ, there's a collision. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/update-set-collisions.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Size doesn't matter.
Descriptions aren't compared.
The creator isn't compared.

source.excerpt: If the name matches but there are different update date values, then there’s a collision.

questions.question: Which update set should you never back out, because doing so can damage the instance configuration?

options.text: The Default update set
Any completed update set
A merged update set
Any update set with fewer than 10 updates

explanation.correct: Don't back out the Default update set; it can damage the instance configuration. Backing out adds delete updates to your current set and reverses record-level and dictionary changes, which can cause data loss. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/t_BackOutUpdateSet.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Completed update sets can be backed out, with care.
Merged sets aren't singled out in the warning.
The number of updates isn't the issue.

source.excerpt: Don't back out the Default update set. This action can damage the configuration of the instance.

questions.question: How many default update sets can each application scope have?

options.text: One
Two, one for development and one for production
Unlimited
None; default update sets exist only in global

explanation.correct: Only one update set can be the default for any application scope. When the default set is marked Ignored or Completed, the system automatically creates a new default set for that scope. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/default-update-sets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: There is one default per scope.
There is one default per scope.
Each scope can have a default set.

source.excerpt: Only one update set can be the default set for any application scope.

questions.question: When merging update sets, which change is kept when several sets contain changes to the same object?

options.text: The most recent change for each object, based on the Updated field
The oldest change
The change from the largest update set
All changes are kept as duplicates

explanation.correct: Merging moves the most recent change for each object from the original sets into the new set. The system decides which is most recent by comparing the Updated field. You can only merge update sets from the same application, and batching is the more robust alternative. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/t_MergeUpdateSets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The newest change is kept.
Update set size doesn't matter.
Only the most recent change is moved.

source.excerpt: The most recent change for each object is moved from the original sets to the new set.

questions.question: Which statement about update sets and the system dictionary is correct?

options.text: Update sets don't track the removal of tables; you must remove tables manually on the target instance
Update sets always delete tables on the target instance
Dictionary changes can never be captured
Changing a column data type always applies, even if data is lost

explanation.correct: Update sets don't track the removal of tables from the system dictionary, so tables must be removed manually on the target. Data type changes are tracked, but the target skips any change that would lose data and logs a message. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/customizations-tracked-update-sets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Table removal isn't tracked.
Many dictionary changes are captured.
The target skips type changes that would cause data loss.

source.excerpt: Update sets don’t track the removal of tables from the system dictionary. You must manually remove tables from the target instance.

questions.question: Which client script type can cancel form submission by returning false?

options.text: onSubmit()
onLoad()
onChange()
onCellEdit()

explanation.correct: onSubmit() runs when a form is submitted. It typically validates the form and can cancel submission by returning false. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/client-scripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: onLoad() runs when the form is first rendered.
onChange() runs when a field value changes.
onCellEdit() runs when the list editor changes a cell.

source.excerpt: An onSubmit() client script can cancel form submission by returning a value of false.

questions.question: An administrator uses a client script to hide a sensitive salary field from non-HR users. Why is this not enough?

options.text: Client scripts optimize the user experience and don't protect data; use ACLs or data policies to secure it
Client scripts only run on mobile
Client scripts can't hide fields
Client scripts run after the record is saved

explanation.correct: Client scripts are meant to optimize the user experience on a form, not to prevent unwanted access to data. To protect data, make sensitive fields hidden or read-only through ACLs or data policies. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/client-scripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Client scripts aren't supported on ServiceNow mobile apps; they run in the browser.
Client scripts can hide fields, but hiding isn't security.
Client scripts run in the browser during form use.

source.excerpt: Client scripts are not meant to protect unwanted access to data.

questions.question: Which client script type runs when the list editor changes a cell value?

options.text: onCellEdit()
onChange()
onLoad()
onSubmit()

explanation.correct: onCellEdit() runs when the list editor changes a cell value. Apart from onCellEdit(), client scripts only apply to forms and search pages. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/client-scripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: onChange() runs on form field changes.
onLoad() runs when a form loads.
onSubmit() runs when a form is submitted.

source.excerpt: runs when the list editor changes a cell value.

questions.question: A client script needs server data when the form loads, such as the caller's manager name. Which approach is recommended to avoid extra server lookups?

options.text: A display business rule that populates g_scratchpad
g_form.getReference() for each field
A synchronous GlideRecord query in the client script
Adding hidden fields to the form

explanation.correct: If you know what the client needs before the form loads, a display business rule can put it in g_scratchpad properties, which are sent to the client with the form. GlideRecord and g_form.getReference() on the client are no longer recommended because of their performance impact. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/client-script-best-practices.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: getReference() retrieves all fields and is no longer recommended.
Client-side GlideRecord is no longer recommended.
Adding hidden fields is the workaround that g_scratchpad replaces.

source.excerpt: a display business rule can create g_scratchpad properties to hold this information.

questions.question: In server-side script, which statement creates a GlideRecord object for querying the Incident table?

options.text: var target = new GlideRecord('incident');
var target = GlideRecord.get('incident');
var target = g_form.getTable('incident');
var target = new GlideAjax('incident');

explanation.correct: To query a table, first create a GlideRecord object, for example var target = new GlideRecord('incident');. Then call query() and loop with next() to process each record. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/c_UsingGlideRecordToQueryTables.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: This is not how a GlideRecord object is created.
g_form is a client-side form API.
GlideAjax calls client-callable script includes from the client.

source.excerpt: var target = new GlideRecord('incident');

questions.question: What does the Record for rollback? option do in the Scripts - Background module?

options.text: Creates a rollback context so the script's changes can be rolled back from Script Execution History
Prevents the script from changing any data
Runs the script on the rollback instance
Stops the script after 4 hours

explanation.correct: Record for rollback? is selected by default and creates a rollback context for the script, so you can roll it back from Script Execution History. Execute in sandbox? prevents data changes, and Cancel after 4 hours stops long-running scripts. Don't run free-form scripts on production. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/c_ScriptsBackground.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: That is Execute in sandbox?.
There is no separate rollback instance.
That is Cancel after 4 hours.

source.excerpt: Creates a rollback context for the script execution.

questions.question: What does the Glide AJAX enabled (Client callable) option on a script include do?

options.text: Makes the script include available to client scripts through GlideAjax, subject to an associated ACL
Runs the script include automatically on every form load
Makes the script include run only on mobile
Converts the script include into a business rule

explanation.correct: Glide AJAX enabled (Client callable) makes a script include available to client scripts, list or report filters, reference qualifiers, or the URL. It's invoked with GlideAjax and users must satisfy an ACL associated with the script include. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/c_ScriptIncludes.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Script includes run only when called.
Mobile availability is the separate Mobile callable option.
Script includes remain script includes.

source.excerpt: Glide AJAX enabled script includes are invoked from GlideAjax and require that users satisfy an ACL associated with the script include.

questions.question: By default, data policies apply to all GlideRecord operations. Which can you opt out of applying a data policy to? (Choose two.)

options.text: Import sets
Target records of SOAP web services
Records submitted from the UI
The REST Table API

explanation.correct: You can opt out of applying a data policy to target records of SOAP web services, import sets, and client-side UI policies. Enforcement when a record is submitted from the UI can't be changed, and data policies apply to Scripted REST APIs and the REST Table API by default. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/c_DataPolicy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A data policy is always enforced when a record is submitted from the UI.
The REST Table API is covered by data policies by default and isn't in the opt-out list.

source.excerpt: Target records of SOAP web services … Import sets

questions.question: Why do the changes(), changesTo(), and changesFrom() methods not work in an async business rule script?

options.text: Async business rules don't have access to the previous version of the record
Async rules run in the browser
These methods only work in UI policies
Async rules run before the database operation

explanation.correct: Async business rules don't have access to the previous version of a record, so changes(), changesTo(), and changesFrom() don't work in the script. The condition builder and condition field still support them. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/business-rules-classic/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Business rules run on the server.
These are GlideElement methods used in server scripts.
Async rules run after the database operation, as a scheduled job.

source.excerpt: Asynchronous business rules do not have access to the previous version of a record.

questions.question: Which onChange() client script parameter tells you whether the change happened as part of a form load?

options.text: isLoading
isTemplate
oldValue
control

explanation.correct: onChange() client scripts get control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading, and isTemplate. isLoading shows whether the change occurred as part of a form load, and isTemplate shows whether it occurred as part of a template load. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/api-reference/scripts/client-scripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: isTemplate shows a template load.
oldValue holds the value when the record was loaded.
control is the DHTML widget whose value changed.

source.excerpt: identifies whether the change occurs as part of a form load.

questions.question: When should an update set be marked Complete?

options.text: Only when it is ready to transfer to another instance
As soon as the first change is captured
Before any customizations are made
Only after it has been committed on production

explanation.correct: When you've finished the customizations and compared local update sets to resolve conflicts, mark the update set Complete. Mark it Complete only when it is ready to transfer. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/application-development/system-update-sets/t_CompleteUpdateSets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Marking it Complete too early means later changes go to another set.
You make the customizations first.
Completion happens on the source instance before transfer.

source.excerpt: Mark an update set as Complete only when it is ready to transfer.
